sections.title: Deciding to start
sections.covers: Whether to start a startup at all: the case for building, the cost of the bargain, and the mindset that survives it.

sections.title: Ideas and markets
sections.covers: Finding an idea worth working on, judging the market it lives in, and choosing the scale of ambition.

sections.title: Starting up
sections.covers: The first months of a company: the condensed playbooks, the accelerator application, and the mistakes that kill early startups.

sections.title: Co-founders and founding decisions
sections.covers: Picking co-founders, splitting equity, naming, and the setup decisions made once: incorporation, banking, cap table, visas, and where to build. The readings are US-centric.

sections.title: Finding product-market fit
sections.covers: Talking to users, shipping a minimum product, and measuring whether the market pulls.

sections.title: Building the product
sections.covers: Scoping the MVP, product design and UX, and the engineers who ship it.

sections.title: Fundraising
sections.covers: Raising seed and priced rounds: instruments, term sheets, pitching, investor emails, and runway math. The instruments and norms described are US-centric.

sections.title: Hiring and culture
sections.covers: Recruiting, interviewing, compensation, and the cultures teams are built on.

sections.title: Operating
sections.covers: Running the company: management systems, founder time, prioritization, and pace.

sections.title: Growth and distribution
sections.covers: First users, growth loops, channel decay, and when to scale spend and headcount.

sections.title: Pricing and sales
sections.covers: Setting and raising prices, founder-led selling, and building the first sales team.

sections.title: Exits and acquisitions
sections.covers: Deciding whether to sell, running an acquisition process, and life after the deal.

entries.title: Before the Startup
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Startups are counterintuitive: trusting expertise over instinct, needing users more than tricks, and why gaming the system stops working.

entries.title: How To Be Successful
entries.author: Sam Altman
entries.teaches: Compound yourself, have almost too much self-belief, and focus: work out what matters most and say no to nearly everything else.

entries.title: Should you start a startup?
entries.author: Harj Taggar
entries.teaches: Which kinds of people are suited to founding, and how someone who is not ready today can deliberately prepare to start a company later.
entries.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; the same talk's official YC Startup Podcast release (December 13, 2022) states the date.

entries.title: Why to Not Not Start a Startup
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Works through the common reasons people give for not starting a startup and contends most are unfounded or exaggerated.

entries.title: Startups are here to save the world
entries.author: Nivi
entries.teaches: Startups exist to deliver innovation at scale, and the services around them have a duty to remove friction from their path.

entries.title: Elon Musk on How to Build the Future
entries.author: Elon Musk, interviewed by Sam Altman
entries.teaches: Musk on choosing problems by their importance to humanity's future, and how he evaluates working on them across rockets, cars, and AI.

entries.title: How to Make Wealth
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Startups are a way to compress a working life's output into a few years by combining measurement and leverage; wealth is created, not divided.

entries.title: Hackers and Painters
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Hackers resemble painters more than scientists: software is a creative making discipline, learned by doing and refined by iteration.

entries.title: It's Time to Build
entries.author: Marc Andreessen
entries.teaches: Attributes the West's pandemic failures to an unwillingness to build, and calls for aggressive building across healthcare, housing, education, and manufacturing.

entries.title: The asymmetric upside of being positive
entries.author: Dalton Caldwell
entries.teaches: Weigh a new startup's obvious and numerous problems against its potential upside instead of defaulting to the cynicism common online.

entries.title: Building Confidence In Yourself and Your Ideas
entries.author: Dalton Caldwell
entries.teaches: How founders build conviction in their ideas while balancing responsiveness to feedback against constantly changing direction.

entries.title: Reflecting on My Failure to Build a Billion-Dollar Company
entries.author: Sahil Lavingia
entries.teaches: After Gumroad missed the venture trajectory, redefining success as a sustainable business the founder wants to run; the aftermath told with the numbers.

entries.title: How to Get Startup Ideas
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Notice problems you have yourself instead of thinking up ideas; well-shaped ideas look like a deep well of demand, not a shallow puddle of mild interest.

entries.title: Zero to One
entries.author: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters
entries.teaches: Build something new rather than copying what works: escape competition toward monopoly, hold a definite view of the future, and nail distribution deliberately.

entries.title: I'm Launching 12 Startups in 12 Months
entries.author: Pieter Levels
entries.teaches: Ship many small products on a public deadline and let the market pick the winner, instead of betting years on one unvalidated idea.

entries.title: The Stair Step Method of Bootstrapping
entries.author: Rob Walling
entries.teaches: Start with small one-time products and a single marketing channel, build to recurring revenue, and only then attempt the ambitious standalone company.

entries.title: The Five Principles of Effectuation
entries.author: Effectuation.org
entries.teaches: Bird in hand, affordable loss, lemonade, crazy quilt, and pilot in the plane: the decision principles Saras Sarasvathy's research observed in expert entrepreneurs.
entries.note: Sarasvathy's underlying paper, What Makes Entrepreneurs Entrepreneurial?, is bot-walled at SSRN (HTTP 403 challenge page); this is the reachable statement of the principles.

entries.title: What's Different about "Unicorns"
entries.author: Jessica Livingston
entries.teaches: Billion-dollar startups differ from merely successful ones in nine ways, including hitting a big basic need, right motives, luck, and founder resilience.

entries.title: Idea Generation
entries.author: Sam Altman
entries.teaches: Train idea generation deliberately: surround yourself with optimistic, idea-dense people and watch for fundamental shifts in the world.
entries.note: The page states no publication date; it notes the underlying talk was given at a YC event in 2018.

entries.title: How to spin your scientific research out of a university and into a startup
entries.author: Jared Friedman
entries.teaches: Researchers commercializing university work must decide who spins out, negotiate IP with the tech transfer office, and leave academia once it slows commercialization.
entries.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; author and text verified from the page's embedded JSON.

entries.title: How to get startup ideas
entries.author: Jared Friedman
entries.teaches: Seven concrete recipes for generating startup ideas, with the common reasons founders wrongly reject ideas; recorded for Startup School 2020.
entries.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; author, date, and transcript verified from the page's embedded JSON.

entries.title: Founder/market fit
entries.author: Chris Dixon
entries.teaches: The best predictor of reaching product/market fit is founder/market fit: founders who deeply understand and personify their market.

entries.title: How to Get New Ideas
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: New ideas come from noticing anomalies, things that seem strange, missing, or broken, especially at the frontiers of knowledge.

entries.title: Causal Formations
entries.author: Jude Gomila, Tyler Lastovich
entries.teaches: Causal formations, per the title; the entry records the citation and claims nothing further about content that cannot be checked.
entries.note: Not publicly available; recorded from the founder's citation as given. No public copy was found, and causal.vc returned HTTP 404 (a Framer "Site Not Found" page) when checked on 2026-10-14.

entries.title: How to Start a Startup
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: A startup needs good people, something customers actually want, and low spending; most failures trace to missing one of the three.

entries.title: Startups in 13 Sentences
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Thirteen compressed rules for the early company, from picking cofounders through launching fast, understanding users, and refusing to be demoralized.

entries.title: Startup Playbook
entries.author: Sam Altman
entries.teaches: An end-to-end primer on idea, product, team, execution, and fundraising, written as the condensed version of YC's partner advice.

entries.title: How to Start a Startup, Lecture 1
entries.author: Sam Altman and Dustin Moskovitz
entries.teaches: The opening lecture of the Stanford CS183B course: why to start a startup (and why not), and the idea-product-team-execution frame the rest of the course follows.

entries.title: Founders at Work
entries.author: Jessica Livingston
entries.teaches: Interviews with the founders of Apple, PayPal, Hotmail, and dozens more about what the earliest days actually looked like, pivots and rejections included.

entries.title: YC's Essential Startup Advice
entries.author: Geoff Ralston
entries.teaches: YC's core advice compiled: launch quickly, talk to users, do things that don't scale, and avoid premature scaling and distractions.

entries.title: How to Succeed with a Startup
entries.author: Sam Altman
entries.teaches: The recurring conditions behind successful startups, starting from a product so good users spontaneously recommend it.

entries.title: How to Build the Future (Mark Zuckerberg)
entries.author: Mark Zuckerberg, interviewed by Sam Altman
entries.teaches: Zuckerberg recounts how Facebook started and advises starting from a problem you want solved rather than from wanting to start a company.

entries.title: Vinod Khosla on How to Build the Future
entries.author: Vinod Khosla, interviewed by Sam Altman
entries.teaches: Khosla on building ambitious companies: a company becomes the people it hires, not the plan it makes, so team and investor selection outweigh the initial plan.

entries.title: The Biggest Mistakes First-Time Founders Make
entries.author: Michael Seibel
entries.teaches: The common avoidable errors of first-time founders, from solving problems and serving users they don't care about to not launching and poor prioritization.

entries.title: The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Eighteen common causes of startup failure, reduced to one underlying error: not making something users want.

entries.title: How to Apply and Succeed at Y Combinator
entries.author: Dalton Caldwell
entries.teaches: How YC reads applications, why 'too early' is usually a misconception, and concrete tips for the application and interview.

entries.title: The Holloway Guide to Equity Compensation
entries.author: Holloway
entries.teaches: Options, RSUs, vesting, 409A valuations, and the tax consequences of each, written for the employees and founders who have to make the decisions.

entries.title: The Founder's Dilemma
entries.author: Noam Wasserman
entries.teaches: The research behind rich versus king: choices that maximize wealth and choices that maximize control diverge early, and few founders get both.

entries.title: How to find the right co-founder
entries.author: Harj Taggar
entries.teaches: Why you need a co-founder, what kinds of people suit the role, and how to find and vet one; recorded for Startup School 2020.
entries.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; author and date verified from the page's embedded JSON.

entries.title: How do you convince someone to join your startup?
entries.author: Dalton Caldwell
entries.teaches: You recruit others by first building genuine conviction in your own idea, because people can tell whether you believe in what you are doing.

entries.title: How to pick a co-founder
entries.author: Naval Ravikant
entries.teaches: Co-founder choice matters more than product or market: two complementary partners with shared history and aligned values, avoiding the three-body problem.

entries.title: How to split equity among co-founders
entries.author: Michael Seibel
entries.teaches: Split equity (near-)equally because nearly all the work is ahead; four-year vesting with a one-year cliff is the safety mechanism, not an unequal split.
entries.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript; originally published on YC's The Macro, December 2015.

entries.title: The Option Pool Shuffle
entries.author: Nivi
entries.teaches: Negotiate the option pool explicitly: investors who put the pool in the pre-money silently cut the effective valuation, with the worked per-share math.

entries.title: How to Name your Company
entries.author: Jude Gomila
entries.teaches: Naming rules from the Heyzap founder: one or two syllables, abstract enough to survive a pivot, and a metaphor baked into the name.
entries.note: The original judegomila.com post no longer resolves; the Wayback snapshot is the reachable copy.

entries.title: The Starter Guide to SF for Founders
entries.author: Michelle Fang
entries.teaches: A map of the San Francisco startup ecosystem for arriving founders: communities, active VCs, workspaces, housing, and immigration resources.
entries.note: Notion-hosted; the page renders via JavaScript (content verified via a Wayback snapshot). The page itself carries no byline; its contact link points to the author's X account, which introduces the guide.

entries.title: How I Earned My Way Into the US (O1 Visa Guide)
entries.author: Sigil Wen
entries.teaches: A step-by-step walkthrough of building and winning an O-1 extraordinary-ability visa petition, from a founder who did it without a degree.

entries.title: What is a Cap Table? Key Concepts & Examples
entries.author: Carta
entries.teaches: Defines the capitalization table, how to build and maintain one from incorporation through funding rounds, and why its accuracy matters for fundraising.
entries.note: Carta bot-walls automated fetches (HTTP 403); content verified via a Wayback snapshot of this URL.

entries.title: The Only Thing That Matters
entries.author: Marc Andreessen
entries.teaches: The essay that named product-market fit: market beats team and product, you can always feel when fit is absent, and the only goal before fit is to get there.

entries.title: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit
entries.author: Rahul Vohra
entries.teaches: Turn the very-disappointed survey question into an operating metric: segment the users who would miss you most and build the roadmap from their feedback.

entries.title: The Mom Test
entries.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
entries.teaches: How to run customer conversations that produce facts: ask about the customer's life and past behavior, never pitch, and never ask whether they would buy.

entries.title: The Lean Startup: Methodology Principles
entries.author: Eric Ries
entries.teaches: The build-measure-learn loop, validated learning, and innovation accounting: treat every product decision as a testable hypothesis.

entries.title: Why the Lean Start-Up Changes Everything
entries.author: Steve Blank
entries.teaches: The customer-development case in one article: a startup is a search for a business model, so test hypotheses with customers instead of executing a five-year plan.

entries.title: How to Talk to Users
entries.author: Eric Migicovsky
entries.teaches: A YC Startup School session on user interviews: extract the problem, its cost, and current workarounds without contaminating the answers with your pitch.

entries.title: 12 Things about Product-Market Fit
entries.author: Tren Griffin
entries.teaches: A synthesis of how Andreessen, Rachleff, and others define and detect fit, including why growth tactics cannot compensate for its absence.

entries.title: How To Find Product Market Fit
entries.author: David Rusenko
entries.teaches: Finding fit as an iterative, customer-problem-driven search, told through the 18 months Weebly spent reaching it.

entries.title: Levels of PMF
entries.author: First Round
entries.teaches: Product-market fit as four levels (nascent, developing, strong, extreme) measured on satisfaction, demand, and efficiency, rather than a binary you have or lack.

entries.title: The Real Product Market Fit
entries.author: Michael Seibel
entries.teaches: Real fit shows up as demand pull (the market pulls product out of the startup); launch MVPs and find customers with urgent problems before scaling.

entries.title: Zero to Product/Market Fit (Presentation)
entries.author: Andrew Chen
entries.teaches: Reaching fit is easier in pre-existing markets with demonstrated demand, with metric thresholds (such as DAU/MAU above 25%) for knowing you have it.

entries.title: Customer convos are the carpenter's hammer // Pick the right tool for the job // Validation Quads v0.9
entries.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
entries.teaches: Customer conversations fit market risk and sales-led businesses; product and execution risk, marketing-led models, and murky future-focused questions call for a prototype or another validation tool.

entries.title: Signal stacking for more comprehensive customer insights
entries.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
entries.teaches: Combine listening conversations, commitment signals, usage metrics, and post-use behavior when judging customer interest; actual behavior outweighs stated intent, and no single evidence source is complete.

entries.title: How to Plan an MVP
entries.author: Michael Seibel
entries.teaches: Scope a lean MVP you can build in weeks: hold the problem tightly and the solution loosely, launch to a small set of users, and iterate.

entries.title: Getting Real
entries.author: Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Matt Linderman
entries.teaches: Build less: smaller teams, less software, half a product, and hiring only when it hurts; the web-application building philosophy Basecamp was built on.

entries.title: Shape Up: Stop Running in Circles and Ship Work that Matters
entries.author: Ryan Singer
entries.teaches: Six-week cycles, shaped rather than specified work, and betting instead of backlogs: how Basecamp structures product development.

entries.title: If your product is Great, it doesn't need to be Good
entries.author: Paul Buchheit
entries.teaches: Pick three key attributes, get those very right, and forget everything else at launch; the original iPod and Gmail examples come from here.

entries.title: Laws of UX
entries.author: Jon Yablonski
entries.teaches: A reference collection of psychology-derived interface heuristics (Fitts's Law, Hick's Law, Miller's Law, the Peak-End Rule) for building products people can use.

entries.title: Building an Engineering Team
entries.author: Ammon Bartram and Harj Taggar
entries.teaches: How early-stage startups recruit, assess, and hire the engineers who build the product, from the Triplebyte founders' Startup School lecture.

entries.title: How to Raise Money
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Treat fundraising as a discrete phase run in parallel with nothing: get the first commitment, create urgency, close fast, and get back to building.

entries.title: How to Convince Investors
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Convince yourself first: investors fund formidable founders making true claims about a big market, not polished pitches.

entries.title: The Equity Equation
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Give up n% of the company only when it makes the remaining (1 - n) worth more than the whole was before; one formula for investors, hires, and advisors alike.

entries.title: Default Alive or Default Dead?
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Know whether current growth reaches profitability on remaining cash before entertaining any expansive plan; fundraising is not a substitute for the answer.

entries.title: A Guide to Seed Fundraising
entries.author: Geoff Ralston
entries.teaches: The mechanics of a seed round end to end: how much to raise, SAFEs versus priced equity, valuation, investor meetings, and closing documents.

entries.title: Safe Financing Documents
entries.author: Y Combinator
entries.teaches: The canonical post-money SAFE templates and user guide, the instrument most US seed rounds are actually papered on.

entries.title: Venture Deals
entries.author: Brad Feld and Jason Mendelson
entries.teaches: Term sheets clause by clause: economics versus control, how VC funds work internally, and how negotiation leverage actually shifts during a round.
entries.note: The book grew out of Feld's free term sheet blog series: https://feld.com/archives/2005/08/term-sheet-series-wrap-up/

entries.title: Invest in Lines, Not Dots
entries.author: Mark Suster
entries.teaches: Investors fund trajectories, not snapshots: build relationships early so each meeting plots another point on the line of your execution.

entries.title: How to Pitch Your Startup
entries.author: Kevin Hale
entries.teaches: A YC Startup School session on pitch construction: lead with what you do in plain words, make the market obvious, and optimize for being understood.

entries.title: Writing a Business Plan
entries.author: Sequoia Capital
entries.teaches: The pitch outline Sequoia asks founders to follow: problem, solution, why now, market size, competition, product, business model, team, and financials.

entries.title: RECONSIDER
entries.author: David Heinemeier Hansson
entries.teaches: The case against the unicorn-or-bust frame: a profitable, independent company serving its customers is a complete outcome without venture capital.

entries.title: The Case for the Fat Startup
entries.author: Ben Horowitz
entries.teaches: A startup's only two priorities are winning the market and not running out of cash, so heavy strategic spending can beat running lean; the Loudcloud/Opsware numbers come with it.

entries.title: High Resolution Fundraising
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Convertible notes let startups raise serially from investors on different terms, rewarding those who move first and breaking fixed-round deadlocks.

entries.title: How to Email Early Stage Investors
entries.author: Michael Seibel
entries.teaches: Cold emails to seed investors should be three focused sentences (what you do, why this investor, a specific ask); short emails get faster responses.

entries.title: How to Design a Better Pitch Deck
entries.author: Kevin Hale
entries.teaches: Deck design for comprehension: make it legible, simple, and obvious, so investors grasp the core message instantly.

entries.title: 16 Startup Metrics
entries.author: Jeff Jordan, Anu Hariharan, Frank Chen, and Preethi Kasireddy
entries.teaches: How investors read startup metrics: CAC as the full per-user cost of acquisition, including referral fees, credits, and discounts, with paid CAC separated from blended CAC to show whether the acquisition budget scales profitably.

entries.title: How to Hire
entries.author: Sam Altman
entries.teaches: Spend a third of your time recruiting, hire slowly, value aptitude over experience, and treat every early hire as culture-defining.

entries.title: Netflix Culture
entries.author: Netflix
entries.teaches: The maintained statement of the management philosophy Netflix's 2009 culture deck introduced: a dream team of high performers, candor, and context over control.

entries.title: How Netflix Reinvented HR
entries.author: Patty McCord
entries.teaches: The thinking behind the culture deck from its co-author: hire fully formed adults, tell the truth about performance, and drop policies that manage the bottom 3%.

entries.title: The Guerrilla Guide to Interviewing (version 3.0)
entries.author: Joel Spolsky
entries.teaches: Hire people who are smart and get things done: a concrete technical-interview protocol, and why a maybe is always a no.

entries.title: Good Product Manager / Bad Product Manager
entries.author: Ben Horowitz
entries.teaches: Role definition by contrast, written to train Netscape PMs: the good/bad format that became the standard way to write any job's expectations.

entries.title: Give Away Your Legos and Other Commandments for Scaling Startups
entries.author: Molly Graham
entries.teaches: Scaling a team means handing your job to new people and finding a new one, and the anxiety that provokes is a sign the company is growing correctly.

entries.title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
entries.author: Ben Horowitz
entries.teaches: Managing through the struggle: layoffs, demoting friends, wartime versus peacetime CEOs, and why most management advice skips the hard parts.

entries.title: High Growth Handbook
entries.author: Elad Gil
entries.teaches: Scaling from 10 to 1,000 people: executive hiring, board management, reorganizations, late-stage fundraising, and M&A, with operator interviews.

entries.title: High Output Management
entries.author: Andrew S. Grove
entries.teaches: Management as manufacturing: managerial leverage, one-on-ones, meetings as a medium of work, and the objective-setting system that OKRs descend from.

entries.title: How to Operate
entries.author: Keith Rabois
entries.teaches: A CS183B lecture on running a company: management as maximizing output, editing instead of writing, metrics pairing, and spotting barrels versus ammunition.

entries.title: It Doesn't Have to Be Crazy at Work
entries.author: Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson
entries.teaches: The calm company: 40-hour weeks, no manufactured urgency, and treating people's time and attention as the scarcest resources.

entries.title: Founder Mode
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: The conventional scale-up advice (hire good people and give them room) damaged founder-run companies; founder mode keeps the founder engaged beyond direct reports.

entries.title: Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Makers work in half-day units and managers in hours; a single meeting can blow a maker's afternoon, so the two kinds of time must be scheduled differently.

entries.title: Marc Andreessen On Productivity, Scheduling, Reading Habits, Work, and More
entries.author: Marc Andreessen, interviewed by Sriram Krishnan
entries.teaches: Andreessen on moving from an unscheduled calendar to fully structured time, delegation, process-over-outcome goals, and systematic reading.
entries.note: Originally published on The Observer Effect, whose domain no longer resolves; this is the reachable a16z republication.

entries.title: How Future Billionaires Get Sh*t Done
entries.author: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel
entries.teaches: Applying the maker's-schedule/manager's-schedule distinction and protecting productive time as a founder.

entries.title: Startup = Growth
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: A startup is a company designed to grow fast; pick a weekly growth rate and let hitting it decide nearly everything else.

entries.title: Do Things that Don't Scale
entries.author: Paul Graham
entries.teaches: Recruit the first users one at a time and give them unscalably good treatment; the Airbnb door-to-door and Stripe install-it-for-you examples come from here.

entries.title: Growth (How to Start a Startup, Lecture 6)
entries.author: Alex Schultz
entries.teaches: Facebook's growth lead on retention as the foundation of growth, picking a north-star metric, and the magic-moment framing of activation.

entries.title: How to Get Users and Grow
entries.author: Gustaf Alströmer
entries.teaches: A YC Startup School session mapping the acquisition channels that actually work for early startups and why growth tactics fail before product-market fit.

entries.title: The Law of Shitty Clickthroughs
entries.author: Andrew Chen
entries.teaches: Every marketing channel decays as it saturates, so durable growth comes from finding channels early and building loops competitors cannot copy.

entries.title: Why Product Market Fit Isn't Enough
entries.author: Brian Balfour
entries.teaches: Opens the four-fits series: product-market, product-channel, channel-model, and model-market fit have to line up together for a growth engine to work.

entries.title: 1,000 True Fans
entries.author: Kevin Kelly
entries.teaches: A creator or niche product can sustain itself on a thousand people who will buy anything you make, reached directly rather than through mass channels.

entries.title: Blitzscaling
entries.author: Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh
entries.teaches: The full playbook behind the interview: which fires to let burn at each company stage, and how business-model innovation drives scale more than product.
entries.note: The short form is the 2016 Harvard Business Review interview: https://hbr.org/2016/04/blitzscaling

entries.title: How the Biggest Consumer Apps Got Their First 1,000 Users
entries.author: Lenny Rachitsky
entries.teaches: Case evidence across major consumer apps that early acquisition was manual and unscalable: going where users already were, one channel at a time.

entries.title: Crossing the Chasm
entries.author: Geoffrey A. Moore
entries.teaches: Early-market success does not carry into the mainstream: pick a beachhead segment, dominate it with a whole product, then expand to adjacent niches.
entries.note: The publisher page bot-walls automated fetches (HTTP 403). Reachable overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_the_Chasm

entries.title: Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave
entries.author: Joseph L. Bower and Clayton M. Christensen
entries.teaches: Why leading companies miss disruptive waves: the technologies start out worse on the metrics their best customers value, then improve until they take the market.

entries.title: The Cold Start Problem
entries.author: Andrew Chen
entries.teaches: How network effects actually start and scale, built from interviews with the teams behind Slack, Zoom, Tinder, Uber, Airbnb, and others.

entries.title: How Startups Die from Their Addiction to Paid Marketing
entries.author: Andrew Chen
entries.teaches: Paid channels get more expensive as spend scales and payback periods stretch, so cap paid acquisition as a share of top-of-funnel and build viral, referral, and content channels alongside.

entries.title: Why Your Customers Would Be Happier If You Charged More
entries.author: Patrick McKenzie with Ramit Sethi
entries.teaches: Underpricing hurts customers as well as revenue: price on value delivered, segment with tiers, and raise prices more often than feels comfortable.

entries.title: Pricing Low-Touch SaaS
entries.author: Patrick McKenzie
entries.teaches: A Stripe Atlas guide to self-serve SaaS pricing: value metrics, tier design, annual plans, and running price changes without burning existing customers.

entries.title: Startup Pricing 101
entries.author: Kevin Hale
entries.teaches: A YC Startup School session on cost-, competitor-, and value-based pricing, why startups should usually raise prices, and the 10-5-20 rule of thumb.

entries.title: How to Sell
entries.author: Tyler Bosmeny
entries.teaches: Founder-led sales from the Clever CEO: founders are the first salespeople, the funnel is prospecting-to-close, and talking to users doubles as pipeline.

entries.title: The Price Is Right: Essential Tips for Nailing Your Pricing Strategy
entries.author: First Round Review
entries.teaches: Pricing as positioning: anchoring, decoy tiers, and why the price you choose tells the market what category you are in.

entries.title: Five Ways to Build a $100 Million Business
entries.author: Christoph Janz
entries.teaches: The elephants-deer-rabbits-mice-flies frame: your average revenue per account determines how many customers you need and therefore which sales motion is viable.

entries.title: The 48 Types of VP Sales. Make Deadly Sure You Hire the Right One
entries.author: Jason Lemkin
entries.teaches: VP Sales candidates vary on deal size, sales motion, and stage fit; hiring one mismatched on any axis fails even when the person is genuinely good.

entries.title: Predictable Revenue
entries.author: Aaron Ross and Marylou Tyler
entries.teaches: The outbound playbook built at Salesforce: separate prospecting from closing, run cold outreach as a measurable process, and staff specialized sales roles.

entries.title: The Sales Acceleration Formula
entries.author: Mark Roberge
entries.teaches: Scaling sales as an engineering problem, from HubSpot's first sales hire to $100M: the same hiring rubric, training, and comp plan applied to every rep.

entries.title: My Favorite Business Model
entries.author: Fred Wilson
entries.teaches: Give the basic service away free to acquire customers efficiently through word of mouth, then convert the heaviest users to premium paid tiers; Skype, Flickr, and Box.net are the worked examples.

entries.title: Notes on the Acquisition Process
entries.author: Chris Dixon
entries.teaches: Startups are bought, not sold: build relationships with acquirers early, create real alternatives, and run the process without deceptive pressure tactics.

entries.title: Should You Sell Your Company?
entries.author: Ben Horowitz
entries.teaches: The two-question test for any offer: is the market an order of magnitude bigger than exploited so far, and will you be number one in it; two yeses mean keep building.

entries.title: 5 Reasons to Sell Your Startup
entries.author: Elad Gil
entries.teaches: The legitimate reasons to take an offer, from an above-trajectory price to founder burnout and market windows closing, and how to tell them from distraction.

entries.title: M&A Ladder: Position Your Startup to Sell It for More
entries.author: Elad Gil
entries.teaches: Acquirers price teams, products, strategic assets, and businesses on different multiples; moving up that ladder changes what the same company is worth.

entries.title: Finish Big
entries.author: Bo Burlingham
entries.teaches: Interviews with owners who sold: the eight factors that separate founders who are glad they exited from those who regret it, starting years before the deal.

entries.title: When Should You Sell Your Company?
entries.author: Jason Lemkin
entries.teaches: Sell when you have a great offer and are out of energy to go big, and otherwise keep compounding; lukewarm sales processes produce the worst outcomes.

entries.title: Rich vs. King in the Real World: Why I Sold My Company
entries.author: Jason Cohen
entries.teaches: A first-person application of the rich-versus-king tradeoff: what selling Smart Bear changed, and how to decide which outcome you actually want.

entries.title: The Founder's Guide to Selling Your Company
entries.author: Justin Kan
entries.note: The original justinkan.com post (November 2014) returns 404; this is the archived copy of the author's 2016 republication.
entries.teaches: Running an acquisition end to end: sell from strength, test whether an offer is real, give diligence data under NDA while refusing team interviews, and spend leverage before the term sheet is signed.
